title: Contains Duplicate
spaceBreakdown:
- unordered_set<int> seen: up to n entries when all distinct → O(n)
- recursion depth: none
- not counted: input vector, returned bool
approach: Scan the array once while maintaining a hash set of values already encountered. For each element, check membership in the set: if present, a duplicate exists so return true; otherwise insert it. This is correct because the first time we re-encounter a value, that value (by definition) appears at least twice. Average O(n) time, O(n) space.
hints: As you read each number from left to right, what single fact about the numbers you've already seen would let you stop immediately? Note that n ≤ 10^5, so comparing every pair is too slow.
Use an unordered_set<int> to record values seen so far. For nums = [1,2,3,1]: after inserting 1, 2, 3 the set is {1,2,3}; the next value 1 is already present, so return true.

```
seen = empty set
for each x in nums:
    if x is in seen:
        return true
    insert x into seen
return false
```

**Smallest input** - only one element, so no duplicate is possible.
`Input: nums = [42]` → `Expected: false`
⚠️ Bug: returning true whenever the set is non-empty at the end → returns `true`.

**All elements equal** - every element is a duplicate of the first.
`Input: nums = [7,7,7,7]` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: checking only `nums[i] == nums[i+1]` without sorting first → returns `false` because 7==7 is actually caught; but checking `nums[i] == nums[i+2]` only → returns `false`.

**Negatives** - duplicate negative values must be detected too.
`Input: nums = [-1,-1]` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: using a `bool seen[]` array indexed by value → `seen[-1]` is out-of-bounds / undefined, may return `false`.

**Large values** - values reach ±10^9, far beyond a direct-index array.
`Input: nums = [1000000000, 1000000000]` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: allocating `bool seen[2000000001]` indexed by value → memory limit exceeded or compile failure.

followUps.q: What if the array arrives as an unbounded stream and you cannot store all of it?
followUps.a: Use a Bloom filter for a probabilistic answer with O(1) memory, accepting false positives; for an exact answer you must keep a hash set, so memory still grows with distinct values seen. Time stays O(n) amortized.

followUps.q: What if you must return the duplicate value itself rather than just true/false?
followUps.a: Same hash-set scan, but return the value when the membership check succeeds instead of returning true. Time O(n), space O(n).

followUps.q: What if every value is in [1, n] and exactly one value repeats once - can you do it in O(1) extra space?
followUps.a: Use Floyd's tortoise-and-hare cycle detection treating nums[i] as a pointer to nums[nums[i]]; the repeated value creates a cycle. Time O(n), space O(1).
